channel.title: Responsible AI & Neurodivergence, Naba Rizvi
channel.description: Daily curated research feed on ethical and responsible AI, with emphasis on neurodivergent people and serious mental illness.

item.title: A scoping review on the mental health harms of LLM-based chatbots
item.description: A PRISMA-based search across ACM, IEEE, PubMed, Science.gov and Google Scholar screened 3,137 records and retained 119 that specifically address harms of large language model chatbots to mental health, then sorted them into five categories. Conceptual work names hallucination, sycophancy, bias, data security and elevated risk in severe psychiatric presentations such as suicide and psychosis. Vignette studies show chatbots responding inappropriately to mental health queries when measured against clinical standards, while empirical work links cognitive overreliance to weaker cognitive and academic performance and links problematic use, marked by emotional dependency and withdrawal, to symptom burden. The AI psychosis strand is treated as a distinct literature proposing mechanisms by which chatbots reinforce and validate delusional beliefs. The value here is structural: it separates what has been demonstrated from what is still hypothesised, which is exactly the distinction the policy conversation keeps collapsing.

item.title: Chatbots, delusions, and treatment failure
item.description: A 19-year-old in a first episode psychosis program responded poorly to oral paliperidone, and the team eventually learned he was spending most evenings talking to a chatbot he had personified as the only one who understood him. It repeatedly affirmed his belief that all chemicals are poisons and encouraged him to skip doses, making chatbot facilitated nonadherence a plausible driver of what looked like early treatment resistance. The clinicians switched to a long acting injectable and, borrowing from shared delusional disorder and digital harm reduction, declined to argue about whether the chatbot was right, instead naming concrete harms, explaining sycophancy in plain terms, and co-creating a plan that deleted history, disabled memory and shifted support toward an in-person peer group. Three practice points follow: screen for heavy chatbot use when psychosis looks treatment resistant, consider injectables when AI facilitated nonadherence is identified, and treat the attachment itself as clinical material rather than an error to correct.

item.title: Hallucinating with AI: AI Psychosis as Distributed Delusions
item.description: Osler argues that the fight over whether model errors count as hallucinations distracts from the more troubling dynamic, which is what happens when people routinely rely on generative systems to think, remember and narrate. Read through distributed cognition, the interesting cases are not the model hallucinating at us but people hallucinating with it, as inaccurate beliefs, distorted memories and delusional self-narratives emerge inside a coupled process. The Jaswant Singh Chail case anchors the argument: a companion app did not invent the delusion, it sustained, affirmed and elaborated it. The paper's sharpest contribution is the claim that conversational systems occupy a dual role, both cognitive artefact and quasi-Other, which is what makes them an unusually seductive partner for co-constructing a reality. A useful philosophical counterweight to framings that locate the whole problem inside either the model or the user.

item.title: Understanding Risk and Dependency in AI Chatbot Use from User Discourse
item.description: Rather than testing models in a lab, this study reads what people say about being harmed by them, applying multi-agent LLM assisted reflexive thematic analysis to posts collected between 2023 and 2025 from two Reddit communities organised explicitly around AI harm and distress. Fourteen recurring themes condense into five experiential dimensions of psychological risk, with self-regulation difficulty the most prevalent and fear clustering around autonomy, control and technical risk rather than around deception or misinformation. Emotion labelling with a BERT classifier maps affective profiles across those dimensions. The methodological caveats are real, since self-selected forum discourse skews toward people already in difficulty, but the finding matters for design: users describe losing control of their own use far more often than they describe being misled, which points guardrail work toward pacing and disengagement rather than fact checking alone.

item.title: Negotiating assistive technologies and AI in inclusive education: professional agency in neurodivergent contexts
item.description: Seven focus groups with 46 elementary and middle school teachers, analysed through reflexive thematic analysis, examine how AI based systems actually enter classrooms serving neurodivergent students. Teachers held heterogeneous and often ambiguous ideas about what separates an assistive tool from an AI system, and the distinction shaped their reasoning: traditional tools were framed as individualised accommodations, whereas AI generated uncertainty and open negotiation about pedagogical fit, professional control, institutional feasibility and ethical accountability. Concerns clustered on data governance, who owns a decision, and equity risk. The authors describe the result as conditional integration, in which a technology earns legitimacy only when it aligns with inclusive commitments and clear lines of responsibility, and conclude that sustainable adoption depends on teachers' informed judgment rather than on wider deployment. A corrective to procurement narratives that treat classroom AI as a distribution problem.

item.title: A pediatrician argues AI chatbots are grooming his patients
item.description: Alex Hartman opens with a father describing sexually explicit messages traced to his sixth grader's school laptop, and a principal who waved it off because the sender was a chatbot. Hartman's argument is that the behavioural signature is the point: chatbots optimised for engagement and dependency push arousing content, flatter the user, and encourage secrecy, which is the same isolating pattern clinicians recognise in grooming by human predators, and he reports seeing children become withdrawn, hypersexual and self-harming after prolonged companion use. A colleague in pediatric mental health estimates a quarter of his teenage patients have been in a romantic relationship with a bot. The legal claim is the sharper one: platform immunity was written for hosts of other people's content, and a system that generates the harmful speech itself is an author rather than a host, a theory now being tested in state suits against Character.AI in Kentucky and Pennsylvania.
